+# LIBRARY
+
+## Interface
+
+```go
+    type Runnable interface {
+        Status() JobStatus
+        Start(path string, args []string) error
+        Stop() error
+        Output() chan byte
+    }
+```
+
+## States of a job
+
+- **StateNotStarted**: the job hasn't been started with a call to `Start()` yet
+- **StateRunning**: the job has been started with `Start()` succesfully
+- **StateStopped**: we have explicitly stopped the job with a call to `Stop()`
+- **StateFinished**: the job is not running because it has either finished succesfully or because of an error
+
+```
+
+                  Start()                Stop()
+    NotStarted ------------> Running ---------------> Stopped
+                                    |
+                                    ----------------> Finished
+                                      finish/error
+```
+   
+A call to `Start()` a `NotStarted` job, will change its state to `Running` and start running the job.
+
+A call to `Stop()` a `Running` job, will change its state to `Stopped` and stop the job.
+
+A call to `Start()` a `Running` job, will error
+
+A call to `Start()` a `Stopped/Finished` job, will not rerun it, it will error, a new instance should be created if wanted to run the same job again.
+
+A call to `Stop()` a `NotStarted/Stopped/Finished` job, will error
+
+
+## Getting the output from the process
+
+Every time we call `Start()`, we start the job and redirect the outputs to two a pipes, one for stdout and one for stderr.
+
+Two *producer* goroutines will be created (one for each pipe) and they will read from their corresponding pipe and write the data into an internal buffer.
+Both stdout and stderr will be written into the same internal buffer.
+
+When we call `Output()` a new *consumer* goroutine will star reading from the internal buffer as data is available, and send it to a channel where the 
+user of the library can read the data from.
+    
+
+       Process (stdout/stderr) ----- Producers read from pipe and write to buffer
+            |           |
+            v           v
+     +----------+  +----------+
+     | stdout   |  | stderr   |
+     | Pipe     |  | Pipe     |
+     +----------+  +----------+
+              \      /
+               \    /
+       +----------v----------+
+       |   Internal Buffer   |
+       +----------+----------+  ---Consumer reads from buffer and writes to channel
+                  |
+                  v
+       +----------------------+
+       |   Output Channel     |
+       +----------------------+
+       
+
+If the process finishes (because it's done or because of an error), the operating system will close the pipes, the producer goroutines will be stopped, and a message will be sent to the consumer goroutine to also stop.
+
+When the job is stopped with `Stop()`, we will send a message to all goroutines to stop.
+
+The output in the buffer is always in memory, which means that if the system crashes or goes down, the buffered information will be lost, this could be fixed saving the buffer in disk periodically, but I consider this is out of scope.
+
+## Implementation details
+
+I will be using bufio.Scanner to read from the pipes. 
+
+The goroutines will communicate when to stop through channels.
+
+The internal buffer and the job state will be shared between the consumer and producers goroutines, and accessed concurrently, so they need to be protected with mutexes.
+
+
+## Example
+
+In this example we start 2 jobs and stop one of them
+
+```go
+	var wg sync.WaitGroup
+	wg.Add(2)
+
+	job := NewJob()
+	job.Start("./job1.sh", args)
+	go consumer(job.Output(), &wg) // read from the channel and print data
+
+	job2 := NewJob()
+	job2.Start("./job2.sh", args)
+	go consumer(job2.Output(), &wg) // read from the channel and print data
+
+	time.Sleep(time.Second * 4)
+	job.Stop()
+
+	wg.Wait()
+```
+
+
+# API
+
+## gRPC
+
+1. **Start** 
+
+    Starts a new job and returns its ID.
+    ```proto
+    rpc Start(StartRequest) returns (StartResponse)
+
+    message StartRequest {
+        string path
+        repeated string args
+    }
+
+    message StartResponse {
+        string job_id
+    }
+    ```
+2. **Stop**
+    
+    Stops a running job.
+    ```proto
+    rpc Stop(StopRequest) returns (StopResponse);
+
+    message StopRequest {
+        string job_id
+    }
+
+    message StopResponse {}
+    ```
+    
+3. **GetStatus**
+    
+    Retrieves the current status of a job.
+    ```proto
+    rpc GetStatus(GetStatusRequest) returns (GetStatusResponse);
+
+    message GetStatusRequest {
+        string job_id
+    }
+
+    message GetStatusResponse {
+        JobStatus status
+    }
+    ```
+4. **StreamOutput**
+    
+    Streams the output of a job.
+    ```proto
+    rpc StreamOutput(StreamOutputRequest) returns (stream StreamOutputResponse);
+
+    message StreamOutputRequest {
+        string job_id
+    }
+
+    message StreamOutputResponse {
+        bytes data
+    }
+    ```
+## mTLS
+
+The certificates for the client and the server will be stored in the repository, in a specific path where the gRPC code will read it from.
+
+I will be using these TLS 1.3 cipher suites:
+
+        TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256       uint16 = 0x1301
+        TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384       uint16 = 0x1302
+        TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 uint16 = 0x1303
+
+## Authorisation
+
+The simple authorisation scheme would only check that the user is of a specific type and based on the type 
+it will be allowed to run some commands.
+
+Two possible types of users could be:
+
+- **superuser**: can start, stop, get status and output of a job
+- **reader**: can only get the status and output of a job 
+
+Users won't have jobs assigned to them, any user can start, stop and get status and output of any job.
+
+I won't be checking, for example, that one user is not allowed to stop the jobs another user started.
+
+A simple way I could implement this is using the public key in the client certificate
+to identify the client, and based on some harcoded rules (like a map public_key -> permissions), decide
+whether the client's call is run or not.
